newsitem.title: USA: U.S. flu vaccine decision delayed, outbreak waning.
newsitem.headline: U.S. flu vaccine decision delayed, outbreak waning.

text.p: U.S. health experts Thursday put off a final decision about the composition of next year's flu vaccine as public health officials reported that this year's flu season peaked in early January.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in Atlanta said flu activity this season peaked in the week ended Jan. 4 with 38 states reporting widespread or epidemic activity.
Two weeks later, the number had declined to 31 states.

Final death figures were not available but as of Jan. 18, the estimate was 8.6 percent of cases resulting in death. Flu is usually most dangerous to the elderly or people with other health problems and there roughly 20,000 U.S. deaths a year, according to the CDC.
The majority of illness this year has been caused by Type A strains.
Flu changes from year to year and the flu vaccine usually targets one Type B strain and two Type A strains.

Experts on a Food and Drug Administration (FDA) advisory panel voted to retain the current Type B strain in next year's shot but decided to wait for more surveillance data before choosing the two Type A components.
Manufacturers, including American Home Products Corp, Pasteur Merieux Connaught and Warner-Lambert Co asked the panel to expedite its decision.
They noted that it would become harder to make next year's influenza vaccine if they did not have an answer in the next few weeks.
An FDA official agreed that "it was very late" to be making a decision.
The vaccine will be developed over the next few months and administered starting next September.
The flu caused by viruses that infect the respiratory tract, causes about 150,000 hospitalizations a year, according to the CDC.
The agency estimates that the vaccine can reduce hospitalization by 50 to 70 percent and deaths by 70 to 85 percent in the elderly.
